slides.title: Goal, opposition, decisions, rules
slides.source: Source: “So You Wanna Make Games”, game design video.
slides.notes: Tennis has all four. Eating cereal has none. A cereal race has a goal, opposition and rules but no decisions, so it is not yet a game. The cereal race is my own example.
slides.picture: Three activities scored against the four components. Tennis has all four, eating cereal has none, a cereal race lacks decisions.

slides.title: Rules and house rules
slides.source: Source: Crash Course Games, “Game Design”; “So You Wanna Make Games”, game design video.
slides.notes: Counts are computed from the rule predicates: 8, 4 and 5 legal moves on a 3 by 3 board.
slides.picture: Three 3 by 3 boards with a piece in the middle. With no rules 8 moves are legal, with no diagonals 4, with a house rule against moving backwards 5.

new_texts: The framework that limits and governs the whole experience.
a group's own change to them
Same board, same piece: the rules decide what the player can choose.

new_texts: Rules a group changes for its own table; they change how the game plays.

slides.title: Mechanics set the tone
slides.source: Source: “So You Wanna Make Games”, game design video.
slides.notes: Blast area is (2r+1) squared minus the cube: 8 cells at radius 1, 24 at radius 2.
slides.picture: A cube on a grid. When it damages the area around it and disappears it reads as a bomb. A larger area feels more dangerous. Movement patterns give enemies personality.

new_texts: Mechanics alone can set the tone: what a thing does tells the player what it is.
No art yet: just a cube. It could be anything.
all_texts: Mechanics alone can set the tone: what a thing does tells the player what it is.
No art yet: just a cube. It could be anything.

new_texts: Deals damage around itself, then vanishes: a bomb. 8 cells hit.
Add one rule: it hurts the cells around it and disappears. The player reads a bomb.
all_texts: Mechanics alone can set the tone: what a thing does tells the player what it is.
Deals damage around itself, then vanishes: a bomb. 8 cells hit.
Add one rule: it hurts the cells around it and disappears. The player reads a bomb.

new_texts: Bigger area: 24 cells hit. More danger, more power.
Widen the blast and the player feels more danger and power. Art and mechanics must tell the same story.
all_texts: Mechanics alone can set the tone: what a thing does tells the player what it is.
Bigger area: 24 cells hit. More danger, more power.
Widen the blast and the player feels more danger and power. Art and mechanics must tell the same story.

new_texts: How a character moves gives it personality: a hop is a frog, a wave is a snake.
Movement also says who an enemy is. Same cube, three paths, three characters.
all_texts: Mechanics alone can set the tone: what a thing does tells the player what it is.

slides.title: Fun, target experience, appeal
slides.source: Source: Crash Course Games, “Game Design”; “So You Wanna Make Games”, game design video; a game design tips video (title to confirm).
slides.notes: Profile values and player preferences are illustrative, scored 0 to 5. Appeal is a dot product of what the player wants and what the game offers.
slides.picture: A radar of six kinds of fun for a mastery game. Step two marks the target. Step three scores the same game for two players who want different things.

new_texts: also: Eight Kinds of Fun (Marc LeBlanc)
"Fun" is too vague. Name the kind: fantasy, thrill, fellowship, mastery, exploration, creativity.
too vague to build or test
Six kinds of fun. A game can offer all of them, but the profile shows where it leans.

slides.title: Art, design and engineering
slides.source: Source: “So You Wanna Make Games”, game design video.
slides.notes: Arrow angles are illustrative: -38, 0 and +35 degrees apart, then all zero.
slides.picture: Three arrows from art, design and engineering. At first they point in different directions. When they share a target experience they point the same way.

new_texts: They depend on each other; results are best when all three aim at the same target.
rules and mechanics: what the player can do
look and sound: what the player sees and hears
Art makes a stealth assassin, design makes a tank, engineering builds a third thing. It feels wrong to play.
all_texts: They depend on each other; results are best when all three aim at the same target.
rules and mechanics: what the player can do
look and sound: what the player sees and hears
Art makes a stealth assassin, design makes a tank, engineering builds a third thing. It feels wrong to play.

new_texts: Agree the target experience first. The three disciplines then set each other up for easy wins.
all_texts: They depend on each other; results are best when all three aim at the same target.

slides.title: Space and components
slides.notes: Space: look, sound, lighting, walls. Components: the objects players use.
slides.picture: A room with a lit zone and a sound ring, then four objects appear in it: a character, a key, a door and a vehicle.

new_texts: The look, sound, lighting and physical setting; it shapes what fits in the game.
The space sets the mood: what is lit, how it sounds, where the walls are. It limits which characters and actions fit.
all_texts: The look, sound, lighting and physical setting; it shapes what fits in the game.
The space sets the mood: what is lit, how it sounds, where the walls are. It limits which characters and actions fit.

new_texts: The objects in the space that players use or meet: characters, weapons, vehicles.
Components are the things players use or meet inside it. Remove the space and they have nowhere to be.
all_texts: The look, sound, lighting and physical setting; it shapes what fits in the game.

slides.title: Clear progress and climactic arc
slides.source: Source: “So You Wanna Make Games”, game design video.
slides.notes: Tension curve: 0.25 + 0.75 p cubed, an illustrative shape. Checkpoint at 50%.
slides.picture: A progress bar with a halfway checkpoint, then a tension curve that rises toward the goal.

new_texts: The player can see how close they are to the goal.
how hard it feels right now
At 50% the checkpoint tells you, and the other team, how far the goal is. Without it you cannot tell if you are doing well.
all_texts: The player can see how close they are to the goal.
how hard it feels right now
At 50% the checkpoint tells you, and the other team, how far the goal is. Without it you cannot tell if you are doing well.

new_texts: Difficulty and tension build toward the goal's resolution.
Tension should climb toward the end: at 90% progress it is 0.80, at 50% only 0.34. A boss at low health should bring the heat.

slides.title: Before you call a design done
slides.source: Source: Crash Course Games, “Game Design”; “So You Wanna Make Games”, game design video.
slides.picture: A checklist of six items drawn one at a time.

new_texts: Does it have a goal, opposition, decisions and rules?
Can I name the player verb and the core mechanic?
Which one kind of fun am I aiming at?
Do art, design and engineering all aim at it?
Can the player see progress toward the goal?
Did I prototype and play test before adding more?
Then say it exactly: not “make it more fun”, but “aim at mastery”.
